notes.body:
The passage identifies a specific kind of spiritual danger that is worse than ordinary temptation — not because it is more powerful, but because it is **better disguised**. The devil tempts people toward what they already suspect is wrong; their conscience can at least name what is happening. But the false preacher — the one who mounts the pulpit seeking applause, moved only by the desire that people weep loudly and tear their garments — does his damage while wearing the face of religion itself. The audience walks in seeking a cure and walks out having been administered more of the disease.

The mechanism works through substitution. True preaching is meant to make the fires of the Hereafter real in the listener's chest — to open their eyes to their own negligence and drive them from their rest. But the applause-seeking preacher gives the audience an emotion instead of an awakening. The crowd weeps together, the garments are torn, and everyone says "what an excellent gathering this was" — and they leave exactly as they came. **That feeling of satisfaction is the injury.** A person who knows they are sick will seek a doctor; a person made to feel well when they are not will seek no one.

What makes this exceed even the devil's reach is scope and repetition. The devil works on one soul at a time. The preacher works on a crowd, week after week, using the very platform appointed for their guidance as the instrument of their confirmation in heedlessness. The text draws a sharp conclusion: whoever holds authority is obliged, as part of enjoining the right (الأمر بالمعروف) and forbidding the wrong (النهي عن المنكر), to remove such a speaker from the pulpit — not as a matter of opinion, but as a religious duty — because what is being corrupted is **the mechanism of repair itself.**

notes.body:
The word rendered "chambers" translates the Arabic حُجَر — the plural of حُجرة, a small enclosed room. These were the literal rooms built along the outer wall of the Prophet's mosque in Medina, one for each wife. Classical Arabic lets the dwelling stand for its dweller; to name the chamber was to name the woman who lived in it.

The shift to "her who was a possessor of certainty" resolves a distinction al-Ghazali plants in the very sentence before. Among the wives, some carried a recognizable human softness: a need for the security of stored provision. The Prophet honored that need by meeting it, setting aside a year's worth for them. But there was **another kind of wife entirely**: one whose يقين was so rooted in Allah that storing grain for her would have been an insult to the trust she already lived from. For her, he set aside only a day's provision, or half of it — the precise minimum, matched to a soul that had no use for more.

The author never names her because the name is beside the point. al-Ghazali is not writing biography; he is writing a law of the inner life. **The unnamed wife is a living proof** that the provision a soul truly needs from this world moves exactly opposite to the يقين held in her heart — the deeper the certainty, the thinner the dependence on worldly store. She is not a historical figure to be identified but a measure of our own reliance on Allah.

etymology: حُجَر (chambers): from the root ح-ج-ر, meaning to enclose, confine, or hold firm — as a stone arrests movement or a wall closes a space. حُجرة is the enclosed room itself. The wives of the Prophet each occupied one such room beside his mosque; classical Arabic named the woman by naming the space she inhabited.

يقين (certainty): from the root ي-ق-ن, meaning to become still and settled, free of all wavering. يقين is not a firmly held opinion — it is the condition of a heart that has stopped shifting. The wife this passage describes lived from that stillness; she did not need the world to compensate for what her heart already held.

notes.body:
The year's provision is not the destination — it is a kindness extended to those who are not yet ready to release it entirely. Al-Ghazali makes this plain by showing how the Prophet distributed what he set aside: some received a year's worth, but only because he saw a weakness in their hearts. Those who had already arrived at certainty (يقين) received a day's provision, or half of one.

What separates the two groups is not virtue in the ordinary sense — it is certainty. A heart that is certain does not need a storeroom to feel safe. It knows, without argument, that tomorrow belongs to Allah, and that worrying over tomorrow's bread is a quiet form of disbelief in His care. The person who holds onto a year's supply is not doing wrong; he is simply still learning to let go.

So this counsel is a ladder. The reader is placed on the first rung — do not accumulate more than a year — because that is where most of us honestly stand. By showing the Prophet's own practice with those who possessed certainty, it points the reader toward what real trust looks like: not a moderate stockpile, but a hand open enough to hold only today. **The year is a concession, and concessions are invitations to outgrow them.**

The reader is not told to feel guilty for needing the full year's provision. But he is told to notice the difference between needing it and resting in it, and to understand that spiritual growth moves him toward the shorter window. The Prophet's prayer — that the provision of his family be كَفَاف, just enough — was not a prayer for comfort. It was a prayer for freedom.

notes.quote: As for her who was a possessor of certainty, he would set aside for her no more than the provision of a day, or half of it
etymology: يقين (certainty): from the root ي-ق-ن, meaning to be firm and settled. The root carries the sense of something that no longer shifts — a knowing that has stopped moving. يقين is not confidence; it is the stillness that remains when doubt has been completely expelled from the heart.

كفاف (just enough): from the root ك-ف-ف, meaning to hold back or restrain — the same root as كف, the palm of the hand, which holds without gripping. كفاف names the exact measure that neither falls short nor spills over: provision that rescues you from both hunger and hoarding.
